To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) a likelihood ratio test is valid for independence testing, 2) a likelihood ratio power test is valid, 3) a power analysis for the likelihood ratio test can be performed, 4) a sample size determination for the likelihood ratio power test can be performed (5) a supervision determination for the likelihood power ratio test can be done, and 6) these results can be used for information theoretic and Bayesian network learning.

(1) a likelihood ratio test is possible for PU-data; (2) the power of the test can be estimated and (3) the number of labelled data required can be calculated a-priori, allowing the user to make informed decisions about the amount of labelled data to collect.

(1) when using a likelihood ratio test, the unlabelled data can be treated as if it was all negative data, but this does not hold for power analysis, and (2) we can compensate for this by using a novel method that can determine the sample size needed to observe a desired effect, and the number of labelled data needed to observe a statistical effect.

the statistical testing of hypotheses on positive and unlabelle d data.
the problem of statistical inference when only positive and un-labelled data is available.
the question of whether or not we can make valid statistical inferences from positive unlabelled data, and how to make these decisions in a principled way.

we have provided the first statistical framework for testing hypotheses in positive and unlabelted data.
